description:
Google Workspace (formerly G Suite) is Google's cloud productivity suite: Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, and Meet in one subscription. The free personal tier covers a single user well. The paid Business tiers are priced per user per month, so the cost scales directly with headcount — a 30-person team on Business Starter pays roughly $2,600 per year before taxes.

That per-seat model is the single reason teams look elsewhere. A 5-person team can often stay on the free tier, but the moment headcount grows the bill grows with it, and the features that justify the cost (custom domain email, shared drives with external sharing controls, admin console, audit logs, data regions) are exactly the ones that disappear on the free tier.

The second reason is lock-in. Years of Gmail addresses, Google Drive file ownership, and Docs comment history create a real switching cost that is painful rather than merely inconvenient. Migrating email, files, calendars, and permissions between providers is a multi-day project with no shortcut.

This page compares the alternatives that are genuinely free or genuinely cheaper, sorted by what they are actually good at — not by who has the longest feature list. If you only need document editing, a free desktop suite covers it. If you need a mail server on your own domain, that is a different problem entirely. Which one is right depends on which Google feature you are actually trying to replace.

painPoints.impact: Business Starter alone runs about $86 per user per year, so a 30-person team is over $2,600 annually and the number grows every time you hire

painPoints.impact: Custom domain email, shared drives, granular sharing controls, the admin console and audit logs all require Business — the free tier is single-user

painPoints.impact: Changing it means a new email address, new accounts everywhere, and a permanent forwarding rule on the old one

painPoints.problem: Vendor lock-in on files and permissions
painPoints.impact: Drive sharing rules, file ownership and comment history do not export cleanly to other providers

painPoints.problem: Requires a connection for most features
painPoints.impact: Docs, Sheets and Gmail are web-first, so offline work depends on the optional offline mode and recent versions of the desktop apps

Keep data on infrastructure you control by self-hosting instead of renting it per seat
Use desktop apps that work offline as the default rather than as an add-on
Break the 'your email is your identity' lock-in before headcount makes migration expensive

Paid entry pricing sits well below Google's per-seat cost. The trade-off is that the desktop apps and real-time collaboration feel a generation behind Docs, and complex Sheets formulas sometimes need rework.

alternatives.description: Trello is a kanban board, not a document suite. steps: Inventory what you actually use — list which Google services are in play (mail, drive, docs, sheets, calendar, groups) and note the ones nobody opens. Most teams are paying for Workspace to serve two or three apps.
Run Google Takeout before you touch anything. Export your data as MBOX for mail and as native files for Drive. Do this first — once you start cancelling, some export paths close.
Set up the replacement for the highest-friction app first, usually mail, since it carries the most historical data and the most external commitments.
Migrate email over IMAP or use the provider's dedicated migration tool. Expect the mailbox to take several hours per 10 GB and validate spam rules and filters afterwards — they do not migrate.
Recreate calendar events, contacts and groups by export/import, then confirm recurring events survived. Recurring series break more often than single events during migration.
Move shared drives deliberately. Folder permissions and link-sharing settings are the most commonly lost part of a Drive migration; document every share before you move it.
Point your domain at the new mail provider and update DNS MX records, SPF and DKIM. Lower the DNS TTL 24 hours before this step or the change will take a day to propagate.

Run both systems in parallel for at least two weeks. Announce the cutover date, keep the old account readable, and only cancel the subscription once nobody reports a missing folder or a broken calendar invite.
tips: Drop your DNS TTL to 300 seconds a full day before the mail cutover. Most of the 'migration broke' panic comes from slow DNS propagation, not from the migration itself.
Migration tools move mail and files far more reliably than permissions. Budget real time for re-sharing documents by hand rather than assuming the tool handled sharing.
If the real driver is cost, migrating only mail to Fastmail and keeping documents on free desktop tools removes roughly 80% of the per-seat bill with a fraction of the disruption.
Free tiers are genuine here — Zoho covers 5 users and LibreOffice costs nothing per user. A team of 30 does not have to pay anything to leave, if document collaboration discipline allows it.

verdict: Zoho Workplace for most small teams moving off Google: it is a genuine free tier up to 5 users with custom domain mail, and paid pricing well below per-seat Google. Nextcloud Hub if data must stay on your own infrastructure and you have someone who can run a server. Microsoft 365 Business Basic when client deliverables must stay in true Office formats. LibreOffice when the requirement is only 'no subscription for document editing' and collaboration is not expected.

faqs.question: Is there a genuinely free alternative to Google Workspace?
faqs.answer: Yes, for small teams. Zoho Workplace has a free tier covering up to 5 users with 5 GB each, including custom domain email. LibreOffice and ONLYOFFICE are free and unlimited for document editing with no account at all. What free tiers do not usually include is real-time multi-user collaboration plus admin console and audit logs — that combination is what you are paying Google for.

faqs.question: How much does Google Workspace cost per user per month?
faqs.answer: Business Starter is around $7.20 per user per month, Business Standard around $12, and Business Plus around $18, billed annually. A 30-person team on Starter therefore spends roughly $2,600 per year. The free personal tier is single-user and cannot be used as a team suite.

faqs.question: Can I migrate my Gmail messages and Google Drive files?
faqs.answer: Yes, with caveats. Use Google Takeout to export mail as MBOX and Drive files in native formats, then import into the new provider — most offer IMAP-based mail migration. What does not migrate reliably are folder permissions, link-sharing settings and comment history, so document every share before you start and expect to re-share manually.

faqs.question: What is the best free alternative to Google Drive specifically?
faqs.answer: For storage and file sharing, Nextcloud Hub if you will self-host it, or Proton Drive if you want someone else to run it and care most about encryption. For document editing specifically, LibreOffice Desktop is free and reads and writes the same formats. For collaborative editing in a browser, Nextcloud Office or ONLYOFFICE self-hosted.

faqs.question: Is Zoho Workspace really free for 5 users?
faqs.answer: Yes — Zoho Workplace offers a free tier for up to 5 users with 5 GB of storage per user, and it includes mail with custom domain support. Storage is the main limit; if your team works with large media files you will need a paid plan or a self-hosted Nextcloud. The five-user ceiling means it stops working the moment you hire a sixth person.

faqs.question: Which alternative has the best Microsoft Office compatibility?
faqs.answer: ONLYOFFICE, which renders .docx and .xlsx more faithfully than LibreOffice and can be self-hosted. Microsoft 365 Business Basic is the only option that is genuinely the same formats, because it is the same software. LibreOffice opens and saves Office formats correctly, but complex layouts can shift.

faqs.question: Is switching away from Google Workspace worth it for a 5-person team?
faqs.answer: Probably not, financially — five seats on Business Starter is under $450 per year, and moving mail and shared drives costs far more in staff time than that. It becomes worthwhile past roughly 20 users, or immediately if you have a compliance requirement around data residency. For very small teams the better move is to stay on Google and stop paying for unused Workspace features.

faqs.question: Does Microsoft 365 cost less than Google Workspace?
faqs.answer: Not meaningfully at the entry point — Business Basic is around $6 per user per month against Google's $7.20. The case for Microsoft is format fidelity rather than price: clients and colleagues expect .docx and .xlsx, and Microsoft is the only option here that produces them natively without conversion.

pricing: Free personal (1 user); Business Starter $7.20/user/month; Business Standard $12/user/month; Business Plus $18/user/month

description:
Microsoft 365 is the subscription version of Office: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, OneDrive, Teams and Exchange mail, licensed per user per month. Personal plans start around $7 and $10 for a family, and Business tiers start near $6 per user. What you get is the reference implementation of the .docx and .xlsx formats — every serious office suite on the market, including every free one, is measured against how faithfully it reproduces Microsoft's output.

That is exactly why leaving Microsoft 365 is harder than leaving Google Workspace. The files are not a proprietary database; they are public XML formats, so they survive the move. But complex Word layouts with tracked changes, embedded objects, custom styles, and Excel formulas with macros frequently do not survive perfectly, and re-fixing them is manual work that adds up across a whole document set.

There is also the endpoint question. Buying the desktop Office apps once removes the subscription, but it does not remove the internet dependency for activation, updates, or OneDrive sync — and it locks you to whatever version you last paid for.

This page compares the options by how faithful they are to Office formats, because that is the only variable that determines whether a migration is a two-hour job or a two-week one. Short version: if you can move to free desktop software, LibreOffice is the safe default; if exact fidelity is non-negotiable, ONLYOFFICE is the better open-source option, and staying on Microsoft 365 is the only choice that produces genuinely identical files.

painPoints.impact: Roughly $84 per user per year for Personal, and more for Business, recurring indefinitely for software that used to be bought outright

painPoints.problem: Desktop Office requires internet for activation and updates
painPoints.impact: Licence checks and feature updates both need a connection, which is a real constraint on locked-down or air-gapped machines

painPoints.problem: Automatic updates you cannot schedule
painPoints.impact: Feature updates land on Microsoft's schedule, and a half-finished update can block a machine for the day

painPoints.problem: Office 365 format lock-in is soft, not hard
painPoints.impact: Formats are open, so files open elsewhere — but complex layouts, macros and tracked changes frequently need manual repair after the move

painPoints.problem: Telemetry and diagnostics collection
painPoints.impact: Microsoft collects diagnostic data by default; the opt-out is buried in settings and easy to miss

Work fully offline as the default rather than as a degraded mode
Keep control of update timing on your own machines
Stop paying per seat for features your team never opens

alternatives.description: LibreOffice is the most widely deployed open-source office suite and the least risky choice for a first move away from Microsoft 365. Writer, Calc, Impress and Base install locally, work with no connection, and handle the common Word and Excel document shapes correctly. The honest limitation is layout fidelity: documents heavy with text boxes, floating shapes, or hand-tuned column layouts can reflow, and Excel macro compatibility is only partial.

steps: Decide how much fidelity you actually need. If documents only ever live inside your team, LibreOffice is sufficient. If they go to clients or external parties, you want ONLYOFFICE or genuine Office — decide this before touching anything.

Take a sample, not an assumption. Open ten of your most complex real documents in LibreOffice and in ONLYOFFICE, and compare them side by side with the originals. This single test will tell you which tool you need and save hours of false starts.

Turn on document telemetry in your current Office install first. File > Options > Advanced reports which documents fail to open cleanly in older formats — those are exactly the ones that will break on migration.
Export your Outlook data if you are leaving mail behind. PST export via the Outlook Import Export Tool, then import into the replacement. Do this before uninstalling anything.
Install the replacement suite on one pilot machine and open your top 20 highest-stakes files. Repair any layout damage now, while you still know which documents are sensitive.

Batch-convert rather than relying on the new suite's open-and-save. For large repositories, a scripted conversion passes over every file once and surfaces the failures in a list, instead of leaving them to be discovered months later.
Roll out to the team with the layout caveats written down. Keep the original files untouched in an archive until the team has worked in the new suite for a full reporting cycle.
Revoke the Microsoft 365 subscription last, after a clean billing period. Export anything you might still need first, and confirm the renewal does not fire.
tips: ONLYOFFICE handles conditional formatting and pivot tables in Excel noticeably better than LibreOffice. If your spreadsheets are the main workload, that alone decides it.
Fonts are the hidden cause of most layout shifts. Install the exact fonts your documents use on the new machine, or accept reflow — no editor can fix a missing typeface.
Keep one genuine Office licence as a fallback for the handful of files that refuse to render correctly anywhere else. This costs almost nothing and removes a recurring problem.
Test one real deliverable end to end, not a sample of unrelated files. Export it to PDF from the new suite and check it against the original PDF the client received last time.

verdict: LibreOffice for the majority of teams moving off Office subscriptions — free, offline, cross-platform, and it reads and writes Office formats reliably for ordinary documents. ONLYOFFICE when spreadsheet formatting fidelity or client-facing layout matters more than install simplicity. Microsoft 365 itself is not the problem if you only need Word and Excel: the one-time Office 2021 purchase removes the recurring cost with zero migration risk.

faqs.question: Can LibreOffice really open and edit Word and Excel files?
faqs.answer: Yes — LibreOffice Writer, Calc and Impress open and save .docx, .xlsx and .pptx, and edits round-trip back to Microsoft formats. The limitation is layout fidelity rather than file compatibility: documents heavy with text boxes, floating shapes, or hand-tuned columns can reflow, and Excel macros convert only partially. Test your most complex real file before committing.

faqs.question: What is the best free alternative to Microsoft Office for Windows?
faqs.answer: LibreOffice is the standard answer — free, offline, stable for years, and available for Windows, macOS and Linux from the same codebase. If your work is Excel-heavy and formatting fidelity matters, ONLYOFFICE is the stronger option because it renders conditional formatting and pivot tables closer to Excel.

faqs.question: Is there a one-time purchase version of Microsoft Office?
faqs.answer: Yes, Office 2021 is still sold as a one-time licence for roughly $150. You get genuine Word, Excel and PowerPoint with no recurring payment. The trade-offs are that feature updates stop, activation still requires an internet connection, and you are locked to that version rather than tracking current releases.

faqs.question: Which open-source suite has the best Microsoft format compatibility?
faqs.answer: ONLYOFFICE. It renders complex .docx layout and Excel features such as conditional formatting and pivot tables closer to the Microsoft original than LibreOffice does. LibreOffice remains the safer choice for stability and community support, so the honest answer is: ONLYOFFICE for fidelity, LibreOffice for predictability.

faqs.question: Can I keep using Microsoft Excel with a free alternative?
faqs.answer: Yes, with LibreOffice Calc or ONLYOFFICE, both of which read and write .xlsx. Basic formulas, formatting and charts translate cleanly. Excel-specific add-ins, Power Query, and VBA macros are the parts that do not transfer fully — if your work depends on them, keep a genuine Excel licence as a fallback.

faqs.question: Does moving away from Microsoft 365 break Outlook and email?
faqs.answer: Moving the office apps does not affect Outlook — that is a separate subscription element. If you are leaving the whole Microsoft 365 subscription, export your mailboxes as PST files using the Outlook Import Export Tool first, then import into the replacement. Do this before uninstalling, since the export tool ships with Outlook.

faqs.question: Is Office 365 or Office 2021 better for a home user?
faqs.answer: If you use Office a few times a month and mostly read and edit existing files, Office 2021 at around $150 one-time is usually better value than an annual subscription. If you rely on the current feature set, work across several devices, or use cloud features like OneDrive sync, the subscription is the more sensible option.

description:
Zoom is the default video conferencing platform: meetings, webinars, phone, and chat in one client, with screen sharing and recording included. Its free tier caps group calls at 40 minutes for three or more participants, and that single limit is the reason most people search for an alternative. One-minute calls over, the host is prompted to upgrade, and the meeting ends.

The paid tiers work out to roughly $180 per host per year at the Pro level, which becomes the dominant cost line for a team that meets daily. It is not an enormous amount of money per person, but it scales with headcount and it buys access to a feature most people never use, because the interruption happens on calls that a free tier with a 60-minute limit would have covered entirely.

There is a second reason to leave that gets less attention: Zoom is one of the most widely criticised platforms on privacy grounds, with its default settings and data-processing practices documented in court filings and criticised by researchers. Meeting content travels through infrastructure that is not end-to-end encrypted on free tiers.

The alternatives split cleanly into two groups. If you want the shortest path to no time limit, Jitsi Meet is free, open source, and needs no account at all. If you want a proper team platform with chat, scheduling and recording done well, the field is more competitive — Meet and Teams both have usable free tiers with longer limits than Zoom, and they win if your organisation is already in that ecosystem.

painPoints.impact: Recordings live in Zoom's cloud with a retention policy you control only through their settings, and chat history exports poorly

alternatives.description: Teams' free tier covers group meetings up to 60 minutes and unlimited 1:1 calls, matching Meet rather than beating it. Its real advantage is that it is bundled with Microsoft 365 at no extra cost for many organisations, so the marginal cost is zero where a Teams licence already exists. The interface is denser than Zoom's and it is noticeably heavier on bandwidth.
alternatives.bestFor: Organisations with an existing Microsoft 365 subscription

Longer free group limit than Zoom

alternatives.name: Discord
alternatives.reason: Free screen sharing and video via GoLive, with persistent channels that turn meetings into ongoing conversation — useful for communities rather than scheduled calls.
alternatives.description: Discord is not a meeting platform, and treating it as one is a mistake. Its strength is persistent voice channels that stay open as people come and go, which suits a community or a remote team that works in the same room all day. GoLive provides free screen sharing with no call-length cap. For scheduled one-off meetings it is clumsier than Zoom or Meet, and recording is limited to subscribers.

Persistent channels feel more like an office

alternatives.name: Whereby
alternatives.reason: Browser-based meetings with per-meeting rooms and no time limit on the free tier — built for people who do not want to install anything or create an account.
alternatives.description: Whereby gives each meeting its own URL that anyone can join from a browser, with no account and no time limit on the free tier. It is deliberately minimal: no chat history, no recording, no scheduling infrastructure. That narrowness is the appeal for one-off calls where Zoom's complexity is unnecessary.
alternatives.bestFor: One-off browser calls where simplicity beats features

alternatives.name: Jami
alternatives.reason: Open source, peer-to-peer, and encrypted by default — the option when meeting privacy is the deciding factor rather than price.
alternatives.description: Jami is free and open source with peer-to-peer calls, so audio and video go directly between participants with no central server recording them. It supports group calls, screen sharing and file transfer, and can be self-hosted. Because it is peer-to-peer, quality on large calls depends on the weakest participant's uplink, which is why it suits small-to-medium meetings better than large ones.
alternatives.bestFor: Privacy-sensitive calls where nobody should be able to record the conversation
cons: Fewer features than Zoom or Meet

steps: Identify which meetings actually hit the limit. For most people it is one recurring call that runs slightly long. Note how often it happens and how far over 40 minutes it goes, because that tells you whether you need no limit at all or just a longer one.

Check what you depend on from Zoom specifically — recording, breakout rooms, registration, custom branding, or a Zoom Room device in an office. Most teams use none of these, and those that do should not switch platforms purely for cost.

Create the equivalent room in the replacement before changing anything, and test it with the two or three colleagues who attend most often. Invite links differ between platforms, so this is the step people skip and regret.

Update recurring calendar invites with the new link. Every recurring meeting in every attendee's calendar needs editing, including ones you personally do not attend — this is the actual work in a Zoom migration.
Update any signage, chat messages, and documentation that reference the old meeting ID. A room number posted on a whiteboard outlives the migration by years if you skip this.
Keep the old Zoom account active for two weeks with the licence downgraded to free. A cancelled Pro subscription immediately loses access to recordings that people may still need.
Cancel the subscription only after a full cycle of meetings has run cleanly on the new platform, and export any recordings you want to keep first — they are deleted when the account closes.
tips: Jitsi needs no account at all, which removes the single most common friction in a meeting migration: people who cannot get in because they never received an invite to a service they do not have.
A custom domain for your meeting URLs is worth doing on Jitsi if you self-host — it keeps the links looking like yours rather than a shared public host.
If your meetings are mostly screen-share-plus-discussion rather than face-to-face, check whether a lightweight screen share is enough. It needs a fraction of the bandwidth and drops far less often.
Do not migrate a paid Zoom account in the same week as a deadline. Call continuity matters more than the roughly $180 a year, and a failed meeting costs more than that in team trust.

verdict: Jitsi Meet is the clearest upgrade for anyone who hit the 40-minute wall: free, open source, no account, and no limit at all. Google Meet is the pragmatic pick if your organisation already runs on Google and twice the limit would be enough. Teams costs nothing extra where a Microsoft 365 licence already exists. Jami is the choice when the meeting must be unrecordable by design.

faqs.question: Is there a Zoom alternative with no time limit that is actually free?
faqs.answer: Yes. Jitsi Meet is free, open source, needs no account, and has no limit on group call length — open meet.jit.si, pick a room name, and start. Discord also has no call-length cap if your calls are informal and channel-based. Google Meet raises the cap to 60 minutes but does not remove it.

faqs.question: Why did my Zoom meeting cut off after 40 minutes?
faqs.answer: That is the free tier limit for group calls with three or more participants. The host gets a prompt to upgrade and the call ends if they do not. One-to-one calls have no limit. The free alternatives all handle this differently: Jitsi has no limit at all, Meet and Teams cap group calls at 60 minutes instead.

faqs.question: Can I record meetings for free on an alternative?
faqs.answer: Jitsi supports local recording free of charge, which means the file is saved on the host's machine rather than uploaded to a vendor's cloud. Discord requires a paid Nitro subscription for recording. Google Meet and Teams free tiers do not include recording. If recording is essential, Jitsi local recording or a self-hosted Jitsi deployment is the free route.

faqs.question: Is Jitsi really free with no hidden limits?
faqs.answer: The public instance at meet.jit.si is free with no call-length limit and no account. Limits come from infrastructure rather than policy: very large meetings can be throttled by the shared server, and quality depends on the weakest connection in the call. Self-hosting Jitsi removes the shared-infrastructure variable and gives you control over data location.

faqs.question: Which Zoom alternative is best for an online class or webinar?
faqs.answer: Jitsi Meet for free and unlimited length, with the trade-off of no built-in registration system or polished webinar controls. Zoom's webinar features are paywalled well above its meeting tiers, so a free Jitsi room plus a shared signup form is usually the more practical free setup. Whereby works too for small one-off sessions.

faqs.question: Is it possible to self-host a Zoom alternative?
faqs.answer: Yes. Jitsi and Jami are both open source and can be run on your own server, which means audio and video traffic never reaches a third party. That is the strongest privacy option available here. The cost is a server with adequate bandwidth plus someone responsible for keeping it running and patched.

faqs.question: Will switching from Zoom lose my recordings and chat history?
faqs.answer: Yes, unless you export them first. Recordings and chat history live in Zoom's cloud and are deleted when the account is closed, and they do not transfer to any alternative. Export anything you need before cancelling, and keep the old account on a free tier for two weeks rather than deleting it — a cancelled subscription can lock you out of files you did not think to save.

pricing: Free basic (40-min group limit); Pro about $15.99/month per host; Business about $20/month per host

description:
Spotify Premium removes ads and unlocks offline listening at around $11.99 per month in the US, with cheaper Student and Duo tiers and a Family plan that works out cheaper per person. What it does not do is deliver lossless audio — even at the highest 320 kbps setting, Spotify streams lossy files, which is why audiophiles and listeners who care about artist compensation end up elsewhere.

The per-stream economics are the part that generates the most criticism. Reported payouts work out at a fraction of a cent per stream, and the exact figure has been repeatedly contested by Spotify, rights holders and analysts. The consequence is structural: a service priced around a flat subscription fee distributes a fixed revenue pool, and the split between platform and artist is not something listeners can influence directly.

So there are two distinct questions, and they have different answers. If the objection is price, the honest answer is that free ad-supported tiers exist everywhere and Bandcamp lets you buy records outright with no subscription at all. If the objection is audio quality or artist payout, the alternatives are Tidal, which streams lossless and claims artist-first economics, and Bandcamp, where the majority of revenue goes to the person who made the music.

One practical note before switching: playlists do not transfer automatically between services, and the free tools that do it (Soundiiz, TuneMyMusic) work by matching track metadata rather than audio fingerprints, so expect a few unmatched songs out of a large library that needs manual fixing.

painPoints.impact: Around $11.99 per month, or $144 per year, largely on background listening

painPoints.problem: Lossy compression only, even at the highest setting
painPoints.impact: 320 kbps Ogg Vorbis is not lossless — hi-res and Masters-quality streams simply do not exist on the service

painPoints.problem: Low per-stream payouts to artists
painPoints.impact: Reported figures sit at a fraction of a cent per stream, which drives most of the criticism about platform economics

painPoints.problem: Playlists do not transfer between services
painPoints.impact: Every switch means re-importing libraries, and automated tools miss tracks whose metadata does not match exactly

painPoints.problem: Cancellation path is deliberately indirect
painPoints.impact: Subscriptions renew through the app store or web with no reminder email, and cancellation lives several menus deep

Own your music outright by buying records directly instead of renting access
Get true lossless audio where the hardware supports it
Put more of your money toward the people who recorded the music

alternatives.name: Bandcamp
alternatives.reason: Buy music directly with no subscription at all — the only major platform where the majority of revenue actually reaches the artist.
alternatives.description: Bandcamp is a marketplace, not a subscription. You find an artist, buy the album or a single at a price the artist sets — many allow name-your-price — and download it. You own those files permanently and can play them anywhere. The trade-off is that discovery is weaker than on a streaming platform: you need to already know who you want, or rely on Bandcamp's tag and fan-following features to find new artists.

Majority of revenue goes to the artist

alternatives.name: Tidal
alternatives.reason: The audiophile option — true lossless and Masters-quality streams, plus artist-first payout economics.
alternatives.description: Tidal streams in HiFi lossless up to 24-bit/192 kHz, which is a genuine technical difference rather than a marketing one, and its Masters tier goes further still. Tidal has publicly committed to artist-first payout splits, reporting a higher effective rate per stream than Spotify. The practical drawback is the smaller catalogue and a reputation for slower app performance, plus the lossless benefit needs decent hardware and a wired connection to be audible.

pros: High-quality catalogue in the classical and jazz space
cons: Lossless needs good hardware to justify the price

alternatives.description: YouTube Music is free with ads and included with a YouTube Premium subscription, which makes the marginal cost zero if you already have it. Its catalogue advantage is unique: official videos, live performances, covers and remix albums that are not on other streaming services. Its audio quality ceiling is 256 kbps AAC, below Spotify's bitrate ceiling and well below lossless.

alternatives.name: Apple Music
alternatives.reason: Lossless and spatial audio at the standard subscription price, with a catalogue that covers classical and jazz better than most.
alternatives.description: Apple Music includes lossless ALAC up to 24-bit/192 kHz and spatial audio with head tracking on AirPods and supported hardware, at no tier above the standard plan. It pays artists the most of any major streaming service by most published estimates, and pairs cleanly with Apple devices. For Android and Windows listeners the experience is functional but noticeably less integrated.

alternatives.name: SoundCloud Go+
alternatives.reason: The deepest catalogue for electronic music, DJ sets, remixes and underground releases that are simply not on the mainstream services.
alternatives.description: SoundCloud is where independent artists, bedroom producers and DJs upload, which makes it the only place on this list with remix sets, unofficial versions, and tracks that were never licensed to anyone else. Go+ at a lower price than Spotify removes ads and enables offline listening. If your taste is electronic, underground, or producer-focused, this is not a substitute for Spotify but a genuine addition.

pros: Good for niche and independent genres

alternatives.name: Deezer
alternatives.reason: The only major service with a genuinely usable free tier — unlimited ad-supported listening, not just a preview.
alternatives.description: Deezer's free tier streams the full catalogue with advertising rather than limiting you to short previews or a rotation, which very few services offer. It also carries an explicit artist payout figure per stream, which is unusual transparency. Go adds lossless and ad-free at a mid-tier price. The interface is functional and the app has improved, though it lacks the polish of the big three.

pros: Unlimited free streaming of the full catalogue

steps: Try the replacement's free tier first and cancel nothing yet. Listening habits are sticky, and a month on an ad-supported tier tells you more than any feature table about whether you will actually stick with it.

Export your playlists before doing anything else, and do it from the desktop or web app rather than mobile — Spotify's playlist export is unreliable on mobile. Note how many playlists you have, because that sets the scale of the re-import job.

Use a transfer service rather than manual work. Soundiiz, TuneMyMusic and FreeYourMusic all map tracks by metadata, and all three will leave a handful unmatched. Expect roughly 5–10% to need manual handling, which on a 400-track library is 20–40 songs.

Handle the unmatched tracks by hand first — they are usually remixes, live versions, or regional bonus tracks that have no clean equivalent. Resolve these before you rely on automated algorithms, since they get worse with more ambiguous titles.
Follow your artists on the new platform even after playlists import. Playlist transfer copies songs, not subscriptions, and you want new releases to keep arriving.

Set up offline downloads in the new app and download on Wi-Fi before you need them. Offline libraries often expire after 30 days on some services, so a one-off download is not a permanent offline copy.

Cancel Spotify through the same channel you subscribed from. App store subscriptions must be cancelled in the store, not in the app, and web subscriptions in the account page — cancelling in the wrong place leaves the billing live. Set a calendar reminder for the final billing date.
Keep the old account un-deactivated for a month. Account deletion removes your listening data permanently, and you may find a favourite or a playlist you forgot about afterwards.
tips: If you cancel through the app store, check the confirmation screen actually says cancelled — store cancellations are sometimes confirmed by email rather than on screen, and it is easy to miss.
Bandcamp does not have playlists to migrate, so treat it as an addition rather than a replacement. Buy the albums you would have streamed and keep Spotify for discovery.
Transfer tools match on metadata, so a library full of live versions and remixes will import worse than one of studio albums. Check the match percentage before cancelling anything.
Lossless on Tidal or Apple Music only makes an audible difference through decent headphones or speakers and a reasonably fast connection. On laptop speakers it is not worth paying extra for.

verdict: Bandcamp for anyone who wants to own their music and pay artists directly — it is the only option here with no subscription at all and permanent ownership. Apple Music if you want lossless audio without paying for a separate tier, and you are on Apple hardware. YouTube Music is the cheapest upgrade if you already subscribe to YouTube Premium. Tidal is the choice when lossless quality specifically is the reason you would leave.

faqs.question: Can I transfer my Spotify playlists to another service?
faqs.answer: Yes, using Soundiiz, TuneMyMusic or FreeYourMusic. All three match tracks by metadata rather than audio fingerprinting, so a library full of remixes, live versions or alternate titles will import with gaps — typically 5–10% unmatched. Have Spotify playlists exported from the desktop or web app first, since mobile export is unreliable, and fix the unmatched tracks manually afterwards.

faqs.question: Which service actually pays artists the most?
faqs.answer: Bandcamp, by a wide margin — roughly 80–85% of each sale goes to the artist, because it is a direct-purchase marketplace rather than a pooled subscription. Among subscription streaming services, Apple Music and Tidal publish the highest per-stream rates, both clearly above Spotify. No service publishes fully auditable per-stream figures for every artist, so treat published comparisons as directional.

faqs.question: Is there a completely free Spotify alternative with the same catalogue?
faqs.answer: Not exactly. Deezer offers unlimited ad-supported streaming of its full catalogue free, and YouTube Music is free with ads and has an enormous catalogue including live and remix versions. What you give up in exchange is offline listening, which generally requires a paid subscription on every one of these services. For pure zero cost, ad-supported listening is the ceiling, not downloads.

faqs.question: Does any Spotify alternative stream lossless audio?
faqs.answer: Yes. Tidal and Apple Music both stream true lossless up to 24-bit/192 kHz, and Dualsayer's Go tier offers lossless as well. Spotify does not — even at its highest 320 kbps setting it streams lossy Ogg Vorbis. You will need decent headphones or speakers and a good connection to hear the difference; on laptop speakers it is inaudible.

faqs.question: Is Spotify worth paying for if I listen passively?
faqs.answer: If you are mostly background listening to music you already know, the free ad-supported tier on YouTube Music or Deezer covers it, and offline downloads are the main thing you give up. The paid tier is buying three things: no ads, offline downloads, and a larger on-device catalogue — all of which stop mattering if you listen at a desk with a connection.

faqs.question: Why is cancelling a Spotify subscription harder than joining?
faqs.answer: Because the subscription is renewed through the app store or web account, and each channel has its own cancellation path — you must cancel in the store for app-store subscriptions, not in the Spotify app. The path is several menus deep on every platform, and the confirmation is sometimes only sent by email, so people frequently believe they have cancelled when billing continues.

pricing: Individual about $11.99/month; Duo about $14.99/month; Family about $16.99/month; Student about $5.99/month

description:
Netflix is the largest subscription video service, and the reason people leave is almost always price rather than catalogue. Plans run from about $6.99 with ads to nearly $23 for the premium tier with 4K and multiple simultaneous streams, and the price has risen repeatedly. A household paying for four people on two screens can be over $250 a year for what is, functionally, television.

The second issue is that the catalogue is licensed by region and rotates constantly. A title available in one country can be absent from another, and titles disappear from the service entirely on a licensing expiry. Anyone who has built a viewing habit around a specific show has learned not to assume it will still be there.

The third is that nothing is owned. There is no purchase option, no download, and no permanence — a title can vanish, and if you were watching it for something other than entertainment, that can be a genuine loss. It is worth noting that Netflix downloads are DRM-protected and expire, so even the offline option is a rental in everything but name.

The alternatives split by what you actually want. If you want volume for nothing, Tubi and Plex carry tens of thousands of ad-supported titles and are free. If you want permanent ownership, that means buying digital copies or setting up a personal media server, which changes the model from renting to owning. If you want a smaller catalogue with family-friendly depth, Disney+ at a lower price point often covers what most households actually watch.

painPoints.impact: The premium tier is now near $23 per month, and a household needing two screens can exceed $250 per year for entertainment

painPoints.impact: Titles available in one country are absent from another, and anything can be removed when its licence expires

painPoints.problem: Multiple streams require the more expensive tier
painPoints.impact: Simultaneous streaming beyond two screens requires Premium, removing the cheapest option for shared households

painPoints.problem: Ad tier pushes the cheaper plans to a worse picture
painPoints.impact: The lowest-cost plan includes advertisements, so paying less often means a worse experience rather than a smaller one

alternatives.name: Tubi
alternatives.reason: Free and ad-supported, with a catalogue in the tens of thousands and no subscription — the highest-volume free alternative here.
alternatives.description: Tubi carries well over 40,000 films and series at no cost, funded by advertising in the same way as broadcast television. It works on every major device, needs no account to start, and has a reasonably good recommendation row rather than just a search box. The trade-offs are the ad breaks, which cannot be skipped, and a catalogue of older and second-run content rather than new releases.

pros: Free with a very large catalogue

alternatives.name: Plex
alternatives.reason: Free ad-supported films and TV, plus a personal media server so you can stream your own files — the only option that leads to ownership.
alternatives.description: Plex does two things: it runs a free ad-supported streaming service, and it turns your own files — a NAS, a hard drive, or a local server — into a personal media library you can stream to any device. That second half is what makes Plex different. It is the most practical route from renting to owning, and Plex Pass at roughly $5 per month unlocks hardware transcoding, which is what lets it stream 4K to devices that cannot play it natively.

alternatives.name: Kodi
alternatives.reason: Fully open source and completely free — the most flexible way to organise and play a media collection you own, with no account and no ads.
alternatives.description: Kodi is a media centre rather than a streaming service. It plays your own files from local storage or a network share, and add-ons extend it to live TV and online sources. Because it is open source with no commercial pressure, it has no advertising, no account, and no phone-home behaviour. The trade-off is that it is entirely hands-on: you curate your own library, and it will not recommend anything to you.

Pricing starts around $7.99 and rises to about $13.99 for the premium tier with 4K and downloads. Outside those franchises the library is thin, so it works as a supplement or a family-specific tier rather than a full replacement.

With a library card you get thousands of documentaries, independent film and educational titles with advertising, at no personal cost. The catalogue is strongest in documentary, science and international film, which makes it unusual and worth knowing about. Availability depends on your library's subscription tier, so not every card unlocks the same catalogue.

alternatives.description: YouTube is where a large share of film and series premieres land, permanently and free, because the creators and rights holders are already on the platform. Its weakness is curation: finding a coherent series among unrelated content takes work, and playback of long episodes can be interrupted by other recommendations. Tubi and Plex curate; YouTube does not.

steps: Decide what you are leaving for. Cost, catalogue or ownership lead to completely different answers, and picking the wrong one means paying for another subscription instead of spending nothing.

Check where your shows actually are before cancelling anything. JustWatch and Reelgood search across every service by title, and this takes five minutes instead of the weeks people spend discovering shows moved.

If you are leaving for ownership rather than cost, start building the library now. Plex or Kodi plus external storage converts your watching into an asset; the cataloguing work is the real cost, not the hardware.

Before cancelling Netflix, check the titles you rely on. Anything on your list that is Netflix-original cannot legally be obtained elsewhere, so decide whether losing it is acceptable or whether you want to keep the subscription for those specific shows only.

Do not delete the Netflix account immediately after cancelling. Keep it active for a billing period so watchlist and profiles remain if you need to check something, and because re-subscribing later preserves your viewing history and recommendations.
Test the free options on the device you actually watch on. Ad-supported services vary a lot in app quality, and a bad living-room TV experience will send you straight back to a subscription.

Cancel through the correct channel and confirm it. App-store subscriptions must be cancelled in the store; web subscriptions in the account page. Take a screenshot of the confirmation, since Netflix cancellations sometimes only confirm by email.
tips: Your local library card is the most underused free streaming benefit available. Kanopy and, in many regions, Hoopla give thousands of documentaries free once you have a card you already hold.

Do not cancel Netflix purely over price while originals are still there — the catalogue is the reason people pay. Cancel only if you are genuinely happy watching elsewhere, and keep a second screen's worth of flexibility.

For children's content, the maths is different. Disney+ at around $8 is cheaper than Netflix standard and covers the franchises children actually watch, which is usually the whole reason a family pays.
If you cancel and later miss a specific show, buying it digitally is almost always cheaper than resubscribing for a month. Keep a note of what you actually wanted to watch while you had access.

verdict: Tubi and Plex for genuinely free streaming, with Plex also being the practical bridge to owning your media. Kanopy if you have a library card and want documentaries nobody else streams. Disney+ if family franchises are most of what you watch. None of them replaces Netflix's originals, so the honest test is whether you watch for the catalogue or for the price.

faqs.question: What is the best free alternative to Netflix with no ads?
faqs.answer: There isn't one — every fully free streaming service carries advertising, because there is no other revenue model. The closest to ad-free at no cost is your own media library: Plex or Kodi playing files you already own, which has no ads at all because there is no commercial service in the loop. Kanopy and Hoopla are ad-supported but free through a library card.

faqs.question: Is Tubi really free, and how does it make money?
faqs.answer: Yes, completely free with no account and no subscription. It makes money the way broadcast television does — advertising, sold against audience delivery. Studios license content to Tubi in exchange for that distribution, which is why it carries plenty of library content that Netflix no longer holds. The trade-off is unskippable ad breaks and a catalogue of older and second-run titles rather than new releases.

faqs.question: Can I watch Netflix content offline or own it permanently?
faqs.answer: Offline downloads on the Netflix app are DRM-protected and expire, so they are a rental rather than ownership — and they only work inside the app. Netflix offers no purchase option at all. To own films permanently you need to buy them from a retailer such as iTunes, Amazon or Google Play, or work with physical media.

faqs.question: Why are some shows unavailable in my country?
faqs.answer: Streaming rights are licensed territory by territory, so a catalogue in one country is not licensed in another. Netflix also removes titles when a licence expires rather than renewing it. Availability is checked at playback rather than browse time, which is why a title can look present in search and then refuse to play.

faqs.question: How can I watch a Netflix show without Netflix?
faqs.answer: Legitimately, check whether the show is licensed elsewhere — JustWatch or Reelgood will tell you every service carrying it in your region. Many Netflix originals have moved to other services after their Netflix window ends. If nothing legitimate carries it, the only options are waiting for it to move or buying it, which is usually not offered for originals.

faqs.question: Which free streaming service has the biggest catalogue?
faqs.answer: Among ad-supported services, Tubi and Plex both carry tens of thousands of titles, with Tubi generally larger and Plex more flexible because it can also play your own files. YouTube is larger still in raw volume but without meaningful curation, which makes it harder to browse. Kanopy is smaller but far more specialised in documentaries.

faqs.question: Is it worth cancelling Netflix if I only watch one screen?
faqs.answer: Probably yes for cost. The ad tier and the standard tier differ mainly in screen count and resolution, so a single-screen household can move to Tubi or Plex free without losing the ability to watch at the same time. You do lose Netflix originals entirely, so check whether anything you actually watch is one before cancelling.
